questions.stem: Which of the following structures is part of the abdominal wall and is innervated by the thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11)?
questions.explanation: The rectus abdominis is supplied by the thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11). The other three layers receive innervation from the lower intercostal nerves (T12–L1).

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is the primary arterial supply to the liver?
questions.explanation: The hepatic artery proper, a branch of the common hepatic artery, supplies oxygenated blood to the liver. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, the splenic artery supplies the spleen, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut. Thus option C is correct.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old man undergoes a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During dissection of Calot’s triangle, the surgeon identifies a short, anomalous cystic artery that runs posterior to the common bile duct. Which of the following statements best describes the anatomical relationship of this artery to the cystic duct and common hepatic duct?
options: It courses anterior to the cystic duct and posterior to the common hepatic duct
It lies posterior to the cystic duct and anterior to the common hepatic duct
It runs between the cystic duct and the common hepatic duct
It is situated anterior to both the cystic duct and the common hepatic duct
questions.explanation: The anomalous cystic artery described is a classic variant that runs posterior to the cystic duct but anterior to the common hepatic duct, making it vulnerable during dissection of Calot’s triangle. Option 1 is incorrect because it reverses the relationship to the cystic duct. Option 3 incorrectly places the artery between the ducts, and option 4 places it anterior to both ducts, which is not typical for this variant.
questions.source: Anatomy of Calot’s triangle and arterial variations

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old man undergoes a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During dissection of the cystic duct, the surgeon identifies a short, anomalous artery that supplies the gallbladder and runs between the cystic duct and the common bile duct. Which of the following anatomical variations best explains this finding?
options: Cystic artery arising from the right hepatic artery
Cystic artery arising from the left hepatic artery
Cystic artery arising from the gastroduodenal artery
Cystic artery arising from the superior mesenteric artery
questions.explanation: The most common anomalous supply to the gallbladder is a cystic artery originating from the right hepatic artery, which frequently courses between the cystic duct and common bile duct. The other options are rare and would not typically lie in that inter‑ductal space.
questions.source: Anatomy of the hepatobiliary system; standard surgical teaching

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old male presents with a 3‑month history of progressive abdominal distension and early satiety. Imaging reveals a large, well‑defined mass occupying the left upper quadrant and extending into the lesser sac. The mass is adherent to the splenic flexure of the colon but does not invade the pancreas. Which of the following structures is most likely to be displaced anteriorly by this tumour?
questions.explanation: A large mass in the left upper quadrant that extends into the lesser sac will push the stomach and spleen anteriorly. The short gastric arteries, which arise from the splenic artery and supply the fundus of the stomach, lie in the lesser omentum and are most likely to be displaced. The left colic artery runs along the colon and would be displaced laterally, the left gastric artery lies in the lesser omentum but is more medial, and the left renal vein is posterior and would not be displaced anteriorly.
questions.source: Principles of abdominal anatomy and tumour displacement
